speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: asked	the Minister for Transport (a) whether any of the MRT's components or systems are operating past the manufacturer's recommended end-of-life date and/or end-of-life operating cycle; (b) if so, what is the planned approach to replacing these components or systems; and (c) what measures does the Ministry plan to take to ensure a systematically timely replacement of MRT parts and systems.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This is especially so for critical components and those with safety implications.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This expectation of the operators is set out in the Rapid Transit Systems Act, the Licence Agreement with the operators and the Code of Practice on Maintenance, amongst others.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: They also jointly monitor and analyse data and trends to try to anticipate any asset deterioration so as to eliminate such risks.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first is a clarification: I am not sure I heard the Minister correctly as to whether he has answered the first part of my question on whether any of the MRT's components or systems are operating past the manufacturers' recommended end-of-life date and end-of-line operating cycle.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My next supplementary question: if a certain part has already expired according to the manufacturer's recommendation, but for some reason SMRT has still decided that they are in working condition, what will be the margin of tolerance that the Minister feels may be acceptable?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would it be six months to a year or more?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My next supplementary question: would the Ministry consider requiring the transport operator to have a proper rail asset renewal schedule for the expired or soon-to-be expiring parts, even if the parts do not seem to be breaking down yet, so that we can stay on top of the curve as far as system performance is concerned?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My next supplementary question: would the Ministry consider publishing input KPIs to measure parts replacement and maintenance works, setting targets and benchmarks against other MRT systems to track not just that the inspections are done regularly but also indicators like the ratio of engineers to the length of tracks and proportion of parts past their end-of-line dates?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My last supplementary question: under the new contracting model, who pays for and is responsible for triggering parts replacement.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If there is a change from the current situation, when will this take place, given that negotiations between LTA and SMRT have dragged on for two years or so?

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: It is quite a number of questions, but actually my reply has contained the essence of what I wanted to say.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Trains are a very complicated system, much more complicated than, say, cars that most people are familiar with.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: He talked about evolution and the way going forward.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: He said we should have "faster legs, bigger hearts and wiser minds", and in particular, the point about wiser minds.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: His point was that when things are simpler, it is possible to distill it into one figure or one rule, and then, we just go "law by law".

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But when the situation becomes more complicated, then you would require judgement, which requires hands-on experience and with time, you will develop judgement because you cannot just simply go "law by law".

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: So, if we applied it to preventive maintenance, cars, especially new cars during their first five years, it is simple.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Anyone who buys a car knows that the dealer will give him a book: first 5,000 kilometres, send the car into a workshop; the next 10,000 kilometres, do this; the following 10,000 kilometres, do that.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: That must take into account various other factors which are included in my reply.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Just this morning, I read an industry article talking about German trains.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: The knowledgeable analyst made a comment that because trains took many years to manufacture and trains nowadays contain a lot of electronic components, and, dramatising a little, he said that there are occasions when as soon as a new train is delivered to the operator, some of the components are already in obsolescence, to the extent that the supplier of the components may no longer maintain them.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: The report talked about the development in Germany where they have an engineering firm who decided to set up a factory to take care of these obsolescent components where no more suppliers want to deal with them.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: In layman terms, you know that some of the early-generation PCs are still functional but nobody maintains them anymore.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: In that case, the operators do have some problems.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: That is the situation we are working in.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: On asset replacement and who does it, that depends on ownership.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: If I own the assets, then, I take charge and I decide on when I should replace them.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But you must have a reason if you want to vary or adopt a particular approach, to decide if you want to keep it for a longer or shorter time.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: There must be valid engineering reasons for doing so and that has to be captured and explained if you are confronted by the regulator.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: The Member asked can we publish KPIs for every component: when are you going to replace this, and so on and so forth?

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But, Madam, as you probably know, I have been spending a lot of my time visiting depots because I wanted to talk to the people on the ground and also see their working life.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: The first time I visited one depot, I was curious to look at their warehouse where they stocked all the spare parts.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Tens of thousands of components, which just shows how complex a train system is.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: So, if you publish for each item and track when you are going to replace this, and so on, I think it would be such a mass of data that I do not think it conveys much useful information.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Let us let our engineers solve it the engineers' way.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: As users, commuters, commentators and some armchair critics, you can just look at it from the outcome point of view; say to yourself, "When I need a train, is it there?" Yes, we are not quite where we want it to be, but we are making improvements.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: This is a top priority for myself, for my Ministry.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Members could just look at me; look at my hair!

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: I think it is mess of duckweed, multiple colours!

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: I promised my wife last night that I will make time to go and dye it before Chinese New Year.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: This morning, when I went to see the cardiologist, I expected it.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Over lunch just now, I was chatting with some colleagues and they asked, "Well, what has changed in the last few months?" They asked if I had changed my lifestyle or diet.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But I can think of one change, which is I changed my job.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: I believe I have answered the questions, Madam.
